analysis.title: Bonds & Stocks Are "Pricing A Fundamentally Different Macro Regime"; Deutsche Is Watching These 5 Market Dislocations Closest
key_insights: Deutsche Bank macro strategist Henry Allen argues bonds are pricing a new macro regime (yields at multi-decade highs, wider sovereign spreads) while equities, the VIX and credit spreads are not pricing the consequences (lower growth, higher default risk). The note says this dislocation is unlikely to persist.
Unless financial stress eases quickly, as it did after SVB's collapse in March 2023, risk assets will come under mounting pressure.

Dislocation 1: French and Italian sovereign spreads widened sharply last week. The Franco-German 10yr spread widened 32bps, the most in Bloomberg data back to 1990, and the Italian spread over bunds widened 23bps. The STOXX 600 fell only 1.1% and is within 4% of its record high, and Euro IG spreads rose only to 101bps.

In the 2011-12 sovereign crisis, March 2020 and 2022, comparable sovereign stress came with sharp risk-asset corrections. Sovereign contagion with limited equity and credit reaction is described as highly unusual.

Dislocation 2: Last week's stress led markets to price out rate hikes from the Fed and ECB, including the October decision. With inflation above target, central banks have limited room to turn dovish, unlike in the 2010s.

In 2022-23 each dovish repricing (Ukraine invasion, UK mini-budget, SVB) was unwound because above-target inflation reasserted itself. Real yields have risen, but broader financial conditions have not tightened much by historic standards.
Central banks tend to overcorrect for the last crisis, and the current reaction function is more hawkish after criticism of underestimating inflation in 2021-22.

Dislocation 3: The oil futures curve is still backwardated and implies normalisation despite being wrong for over six months. Brent front-end is $102/bbl, the 6-month is $90 and the 12-month is $83. The December 2026 contract is near its highest level to date.
The curve fell in June on the interim US-Iran deal, then became backwardated again after the re-escalation from July onwards.

Dislocation 4: Markets price the first-round inflation shock from the Strait of Hormuz closure (energy and food) but not second-round effects. Brent has stayed above $100/bbl, and El Nino risks adding to food prices.

Five reasons given for second-round risk: no obvious path to a sharp oil decline (reports of possible resumed bombing after the mid-terms and an extra US carrier group deployed to the Persian Gulf), supply shocks can linger (1973 oil prices stayed near 4x in real terms for years), energy inflation spread into core in 2021-22, tightening effects peak after about 12 months, and prolonged above-target inflation raises the risk of unanchored expectations.

Dislocation 5: Yields are at multi-year highs globally on inflation, fiscal and policy-rate risk, yet the S&P 500 closed within 1% of its record high last Friday and the STOXX 600 is within 4% of its high. Last week's moves show this is no longer only a strong-growth story, with sovereign spreads widening, credit coming under stress and doubts about the economy coping with more hikes.
Equity reactions to stress can lag. In late 2021 the S&P 500 and STOXX 600 kept rising until January 2022 despite hawkish central banks and high inflation.

Conclusion: resolution depends on whether financial stress slows the economy. If stress continues, precedent suggests risk assets come under pressure with a lag. SVB 2023 is the counterexample where stress passed quickly.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Largest weekly widening in Bloomberg data back to 1990. The spread is at its widest since 2012, signalling contagion fears that equities have not matched.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Confirms sovereign stress in Europe's periphery that rates markets are pricing and risk assets are not.
Small decline relative to the spread widening, with the index within 4% of its record high.
Far below levels seen in 2011-12, 2020 and 2022, so credit is not pricing the sovereign stress.
Oil is holding above $100 because of the Strait of Hormuz disruption.
The curve implies a decline in six months that has not materialised in prior months.
Backwardation shows markets still pricing a resolution of the conflict.

risk_factors: Equities and credit repricing to catch up with bond-market stress.
Dovish central bank repricings unwinding because inflation is above target.
Second-round inflation effects from prolonged energy supply shock, possibly unanchoring inflation expectations.
Further escalation in the Persian Gulf and a longer Strait of Hormuz closure.
Fiscal risk and European sovereign contagion (France, Italy).
Lagged effect of monetary tightening, which peaks after about 12 months.
vol_and_positioning: VIX remains subdued despite bond market stress.
Euro IG spreads at 101bps and global credit spreads are well below recent-year highs.
Commodity curves price oil normalisation next year and beyond.
geopolitical: US-Iran conflict now over six months old, with the Strait of Hormuz still restricted.
Interim US-Iran deal agreed in June, followed by re-escalation from July onwards.
WSJ reported President Trump expects to resume bombing after the mid-terms.
Bloomberg and others reported the US is sending an additional aircraft carrier plus 10,000 sailors and Marines to the Persian Gulf.

tension_points.bull_case: Equities and credit are shrugging off stress. The S&P 500 is within 1% of its high and the STOXX 600 within 4%, and past episodes such as SVB in March 2023 passed quickly without a broader correction.
tension_points.bear_case: Bonds price contagion, higher inflation and rate risk, while sovereign spreads widen, credit is under stress and oil is above $100. In 2011-12, 2020 and 2022 comparable stress led to significant equity declines, with a lag.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Financial stress easing rapidly, as after SVB's collapse in March 2023, would invalidate the bearish case.

tension_points.bull_case: Futures curve implies Brent falls from $102 to $90 in six months and $83 in twelve if the Strait of Hormuz reopens.
tension_points.bear_case: The curve has been wrong for six months. A restricted Strait, possible escalation and past supply shocks suggest prices stay high and second-round inflation follows.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A breakthrough in the US-Iran conflict reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

theme_stances.key_argument: Bonds price the symptoms of a new regime without equities pricing the consequences, and this dislocation is unlikely to persist.
theme_stances.evidence: This dislocation is unlikely to persist.

theme_stances.key_argument: With inflation above target, central banks cannot turn dovish at every bout of financial stress, so priced-out hikes risk being reversed.
theme_stances.evidence: there's inherently a limit to how dovish central banks can become

theme_stances.key_argument: The curve keeps pricing a normalisation that has not arrived, and risks lean toward higher and more persistent oil prices.
theme_stances.evidence: Markets keep pricing a breakthrough that hasn't arrived.
